To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
low‐dose (10 Gy) preoperative radiotherapy was effective in the adjuvant treatment of patients with clinical stage I endometrial cancer.
low‐dose radiation therapy (10 Gy in 4 days) is an appropriate treatment for Stage I, grade I and II endometrial carcinoma.
preoperative radiation therapy in patients with clinical stage I, grade 3 or 4 endometrial carcinoma does not appear to be beneficial.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of low‐dosedose radiation therapy as a preoperative procedure for clinical Stage I (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics [FIGO] Stage I) adenocarcinomas of the endometrial.
the development of a treatment policy using low‐doses of preoperative radiation therapy.
the use of low‐dosing radiation therapy as a method of treatment of cancer of the endometrial.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
preoperative low‐dose radiation therapy is not indicated for the treatment of adenocarcinomas of the endometrial.
low‐dose radiation therapy is not indicated as an adjunct to surgery in the treatment of endometrial cancer.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 4‐year survival and disease‐free rates for clinical Stage I endometrial cancer are comparable to those reported by others using more aggressive radiotherapy, but with fewer complications.

the 4‐year survival rate for the group with clinical Stage I was 80%; the disease‐free rate in the same group was 77%; and the corresponding rates for Stage I disease found by pathologic examination were 96% and 94%, respectively.

the use of low‐doses of preoperative radiation therapy (10 Gy in 4 days) in patients with clinical Stage 1 adenocarcinomas of the endometria is a useful procedure in that the patients are spared a more extensive surgical procedure and postoperative radiation therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of preoperative radiotherapy for endometrial cancer has been associated with a significant increase in the rate of complications and that the use of postoperative radiotherapy is associated with a higher rate of complications compared to no radiotherapy at all.
preoperative radiation therapy may be used to reduce the risk of recurrence in patients with clinical Stage II, III, or IV disease.
preoperative radiation therapy should be considered for all endometrial cancer patients with high risk factors.
